author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.1 (Schwartz/Loeb section 1)
original: Ἐπειδὴ δὲ τὴν περὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ γενεαλογίαν διαφόρως ἡμῖν ὅ τε Ματθαῖος καὶ ὁ Λουκᾶς εὐαγγελιζόμενοι παραδεδώκασι, διαφωνεῖν τε νομίζονται τοῖς πολλοῖς, τῶν τε πιστῶν ἕκαστος ἀγνοίᾳ τἀληθοῦς εὑρησιλογεῖν εἰς τοὺς τόπους πεφιλοτίμηται, φέρε, καὶ τὴν περὶ τούτων καταελθοῦσαν εἰς ἡμᾶς ἱστορίαν παραθώμεθα, ἣν δι' ἐπιστολῆς Ἀριστείδῃ γράφων περὶ συμφωνίας τῆς ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις γενεαλογίας ὁ μικρῷ πρόσθεν ἡμῖν δηλωθεὶς Ἀφρικανὸς ἐμνημόνευσεν
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: Matthew and Luke in their gospels have given us the genealogy of Christ differently, and many suppose that they are at variance with one another. Since as a consequence every believer, in ignorance of the truth, has been zealous to invent some explanation which shall harmonize the two passages, permit us to subjoin the account of the matter which has come down to us, and which is given by Africanus, who was mentioned by us just above, in his epistle to Aristides, where he discusses the harmony of the gospel genealogies.
edition: W. Heinemann / Putnam, London/New York 1926 (archive.org eusebiustheeccle0001unse)
what_it_says: Eusebius introduces Africanus's letter to Aristides as the earliest account of how the two gospel genealogies fit together.
limits: Eusebius's own framing; Africanus's text starts at section 2. Does not say which account Africanus got from tradition in detail.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.2 (Loeb section 2)
original: “Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν γενῶν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ἠριθμεῖτο ἢ φύσει ἢ νόμῳ, φύσει μέν, γνησίου σπέρματος διαδοχῇ, νόμῳ δέ, ἑτέρου παιδοποιουμένου εἰς ὄνομα τελευτήσαντος ἀδελφοῦ ἀτέκνου (ὅτι γὰρ οὐδέπω δέδοτο ἐλπὶς ἀναστάσεως σαφής, τὴν μέλλουσαν ἐπαγγελίαν ἀναστάσει ἐμιμοῦντο θνητῇ, ἵνα ἀνέκλειπτον τὸ ὄνομα μείνῃ τοῦ μετηλλαχότος)·”
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: For whereas the names of the generations were reckoned in Israel either according to nature or according to law — according to nature by the succession of legitimate offspring, and according to law whenever another raised up a child to the name of a brother dying childless; for because a clear hope of resurrection was not yet given they had a representation of the future promise by a kind of mortal resurrection, in order that the name of the one deceased might be perpetuated —
what_it_says: Africanus says that Israelite genealogies were counted by nature (real descent) or by law (a childless brother's name raised up through a levirate-type marriage).
limits: The levirate ('raise up seed') rule is Africanus's premise; the Loeb note 1 (p. 56) says the Greek 'deaths of the childless' reading is an Eusebian copying error per cod. q of the Quaestiones ad Stephanum; not checked against that codex.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.4-5 (Loeb sections 4-5)
original: οὕτως οὐδέτερον τῶν εὐαγγελίων ψεύδεται, καὶ φύσιν ἀριθμοῦν καὶ νόμον. ἐπεπλάκη γὰρ ἀλλήλοις τὰ γένη, τό τε ἀπὸ τοῦ Σολομῶνος καὶ τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ναθάν, ἀναστάσεσιν ἀτέκνων καὶ δευτερογαμίαις καὶ ἀναστάσει σπερμάτων, ὡς δικαίως τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἄλλοτε ἄλλων νομίζεσθαι, τῶν μὲν δοκούντων πατέρων, τῶν δὲ ὑπαρχόντων· ὡς ἀμφοτέρας τὰς διηγήσεις κυρίως ἀληθεῖς οὔσας ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰωσὴφ πολυπλόκως μέν, ἀλλ' ἀκριβῶς κατελθεῖν. [§5] ἀπὸ τοῦ Δαυὶδ διὰ Σολομῶνος τὰς γενεὰς καταριθμουμένοις τρίτος ἀπὸ τέλους εὑρίσκεται Ματθάν, ὃς ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰακώβ, τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν πατέρα· ἀπὸ δὲ Ναθὰν τοῦ Δαυὶδ κατὰ Λουκᾶν ὁμοίως τρίτος ἀπὸ τέλους Μελχί· Ἰωσὴφ γὰρ υἱὸς Ἡλὶ τοῦ Μελχί.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: 4. Thus neither of the gospels is in error, for one reckons by nature, the other by law. For the line of descent from Solomon and that from Nathan were so involved, the one with the other, by the raising up of children to the childless and by second marriages, that the same persons are justly considered to belong at one time to one, at another time to another; that is, at one time to the reputed fathers, at another to the actual fathers. So that both these accounts are strictly true and come down to Joseph with considerable intricacy indeed, yet quite accurately. 5. ... If we reckon the generations from David through Solomon, the third from the end is found to be Matthan, who begot Jacob the father of Joseph. But if, with Luke, we reckon them from Nathan the son of David, in like manner the third from the end is Melchi, whose son Eli was the father of Joseph. For Joseph was the son of Eli, the son of Melchi.
what_it_says: Africanus's core claim: both genealogies are true, one by nature and one by law, because the Solomon and Nathan lines were interwoven by levirate marriages; Matthan (Solomon line) and Melchi (Nathan line) are both grandfathers of Joseph in different senses.
limits: Africanus does not give Luke's or Matthew's explicit line for Mary; this is a claim about Joseph only.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.7-8 (Loeb sections 7-8)
original: καὶ δὴ οὖν ὅ τε Ματθὰν καὶ ὁ Μελχί, ἐν μέρει τὴν αὐτὴν ἀγαγόμενοι γυναῖκα, ὁμομητρίους ἀδελφοὺς ἐπαιδοποιήσαντο, τοῦ νόμου μὴ κωλύοντος χηρεύουσαν, ἤτοι ἀπολελυμένην ἢ καὶ τελευτήσαντος τοῦ ἀνδρός, ἄλλῳ γαμεῖσθαι. ἐκ δὴ τῆς Ἐσθὰ (τοῦτο γὰρ καλεῖσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα παραδέδοται) πρῶτος Ματθάν, ὁ ἀπὸ τοῦ Σολομῶνος τὸ γένος κατάγων, τὸν Ἰακὼβ γεννᾷ, καὶ τελευτήσαντος τοῦ Ματθὰν Μελχί, ὁ ἐπὶ τὸν Ναθὰν κατὰ γένος ἀναφερόμενος, χηρεύουσαν, ἐκ μὲν τῆς αὐτῆς φυλῆς, ἐξ ἄλλου δὲ γένους ὤν, ὡς προεἶπον, ἀγαγόμενος αὐτήν, ἔσχεν υἱὸν τὸν Ἡλί.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: 7. Matthan and Melchi having married in succession the same woman, begot children who were uterine brothers, for the law did not prohibit a widow, whether such by divorce or by the death of her husband, from marrying another. 8. By Estha then (for this was the woman's name according to tradition) Matthan, a descendant of Solomon, first begot Jacob. And when Matthan was dead, Melchi, who traced his descent back to Nathan, being of the same tribe but of another family, married her as before said, and begot a son Eli.
what_it_says: Africanus names the mother as Estha (by tradition), says Matthan and Melchi were successive husbands of one woman, and that Jacob and Eli were uterine brothers.
limits: The 'Estha' name and the uterine-brother claim rest on 'tradition' as Africanus says; no Scripture cited. Note: Melchi is said to be 'of the same tribe' but another family (Africanus's wording).

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.9 (Loeb section 9; Africanus cites Matt 1:16)
original: οὕτω δὴ διαφόρων δύο γενῶν εὑρήσομεν τόν τε Ἰακὼβ καὶ τὸν Ἡλὶ ὁμομητρίους ἀδελφούς, ὧν ὁ ἕτερος, Ἰακὼβ, ἀτέκνου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τελευτήσαντος Ἡλί, τὴν γυναῖκα παραλαβών, ἐγέννησεν ἐξ αὐτῆς τρίτον τὸν Ἰωσήφ, κατὰ φύσιν μὲν ἑαυτῷ (καὶ κατὰ λόγον, δι' ὃ γέγραπται ‘Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωσήφ’), κατὰ νόμον δὲ τοῦ Ἡλὶ υἱὸς ἦν· ἐκείνῳ γὰρ ὁ Ἰακώβ, ἀδελφὸς ὢν, ἀνέστησεν σπέρμα.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: Thus we shall find the two, Jacob and Eli, although belonging to different families, yet brethren by the same mother. Of these the one, Jacob, when his brother Eli had died childless, took the latter's wife and begot by her a son Joseph, his own son by nature and in accordance with reason. Wherefore also it is written: 'Jacob begot Joseph.' [NPNF2 inserts 'Matthew 1:6'; the Greek cites Matt 1:16] But according to law he was the son of Eli, for Jacob, being the brother of the latter, raised up seed to him.
what_it_says: Africanus's solution: Jacob (Matthew's father of Joseph) and Eli (Luke's father) were uterine brothers, Eli died childless, and Jacob raised seed to him, so Joseph was Jacob's son by nature and Eli's son by law.
limits: The Greek has the word τρίτον ('third') after 'by her' that NPNF2 omits; its sense is unclear and is not explained here. This is the central Africanus/Eusebius adoption-by-levirate claim; it is an interpretation, not a witness about Mary.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.10 (Loeb section 10; Luke 3:23, 3:38)
original: ἣν Ματθαῖος μὲν ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς ἐξαριθμούμενος ‘Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωσήφ,’ ὁ δὲ Λουκᾶς ἀνάπαλιν ‘ὃς ἦν, ὡς ἐνομίζετο (καὶ γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο προστίθησιν) τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τοῦ Ἡλὶ τοῦ Μελχί.’ τὴν γὰρ κατὰ νόμον γένεσιν ἐπισημότερον οὐκ ἦν ἐξειπεῖν, καὶ τὸ ‘ἐγέννησεν’ ἐπὶ τῆς τοιᾶσδε παιδοποιίας ἄχρι τέλους ἐσιώπησεν, τὴν ἀναφορὰν ποιησάμενος ἕως ‘τοῦ Ἀδὰμ τοῦ θεοῦ’ κατ' ἀνάλυσιν.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: Hence the genealogy traced through him will not be rendered void, which the evangelist Matthew in his enumeration gives thus: 'Jacob begot Joseph.' But Luke, on the other hand, says: 'Who was the son, as was supposed' (for this he also adds), 'of Joseph, the son of Eli, the son of Melchi'; for he could not more clearly express the generation according to law. And the expression 'he begot' he has omitted in his genealogical table up to the end, tracing the genealogy back to Adam the son of God.
what_it_says: Africanus reads Luke's 'as was supposed' (ὡς ἐνομίζετο) as marking the legal line and notes Luke drops 'begot' throughout, running up to Adam.
limits: Africanus's reading of Luke's wording is his own reconstruction; the text says nothing about Mary's line or about Heli being her father.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.11 (Loeb section 11)
original: οὐδὲ ἀναπόδεικτον ἢ ἐσχεδιασμένον ἐστὶν τοῦτο. τοῦ γοῦν σωτῆρος οἱ κατὰ σάρκα συγγενεῖς, εἴτ' οὖν φανητιῶντες εἴθ' ἁπλῶς ἐκδιδάσκοντες, πάντως δὲ ἀληθεύοντες, παρέδοσαν καὶ ταῦτα· ὡς Ἰδουμαῖοι λῃσταὶ Ἀσκάλωνι πόλει τῆς Παλαιστίνης ἐπελθόντες, ἐξ εἰδωλείου Ἀπόλλωνος, ὃ πρὸς τοῖς τείχεσιν ἵδρυτο, Ἀντίπατρον Ἡρῴδου τινὸς ἱεροδούλου παῖδα πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις σύλοις αἰχμάλωτον ἀπῆγον
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: For the relatives of our Lord according to the flesh, whether with the desire of boasting or simply wishing to state the fact, in either case truly, have handed down the following account: Some Idumean robbers, having attacked Ascalon, a city of Palestine, carried away from a temple of Apollo which stood near the walls, in addition to other booty, Antipater, son of a certain temple slave named Herod.
what_it_says: Africanus says the source of his account is the Lord's blood relatives (the 'desposyni' tradition), and gives an origin story for Herod's father Antipater.
limits: Africanus says the relatives were speaking truthfully but cites no document in this passage; the Herod story is not about Mary's lineage.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.13 (Loeb section 13)
original: ἐνέπρησεν αὐτῶν τὰς ἀναγραφὰς τῶν γενῶν, οἰόμενος εὐγενὴς ἀναφανεῖσθαι τῷ μηδ' ἄλλον ἔχειν ἐκ δημοσίου συγγραφῆς τὸ γένος ἀνάγειν ἐπὶ τοὺς πατριάρχας ἢ προσηλύτους τούς τε καλουμένους γειώρας, τοὺς ἐπιμίκτους.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: ...Herod, inasmuch as the lineage of the Israelites contributed nothing to his advantage, and since he was goaded with the consciousness of his own ignoble extraction, burned all the genealogical records, thinking that he might appear of noble origin if no one else were able, from the public registers, to trace back his lineage to the patriarchs or proselytes and to those mingled with them, who were called Georae.
what_it_says: Africanus says Herod burned the public genealogical archives, so that after him only private family records (or memory) could trace descent.
limits: Africanus's account of Herod's motive is his interpretation. It is the reason he gives for why public genealogies were lost; not evidence about Mary.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.14 (Loeb section 14)
original: ὀλίγοι δὴ τῶν ἐπιμελῶν, ἰδιωτικὰς ἑαυτοῖς ἀπογραφὰς ἢ μνημονεύσαντες τῶν ὀνομάτων ἢ ἄλλως ἔχοντες ἐξ ἀντιγράφων, ἐναβρύνονται σωζομένῃ τῇ μνήμῃ τῆς εὐγενείας· ὧν ἐτύγχανον οἱ προειρημένοι, δεσπόσυνοι καλούμενοι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ σωτήριον γένος συνάφειαν ἀπό τε Ναζάρων καὶ Κωχαβα κωμῶν Ἰουδαϊκῶν τῇ λοιπῇ γῇ ἐπιφοιτήσαντες
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: A few of the careful, however, having obtained private records of their own, either by remembering the names or by getting them in some other way from the registers, pride themselves on preserving the memory of their noble extraction. Among these are those already mentioned, called Desposyni, on account of their connection with the family of the Saviour. Coming from Nazara and Cochaba, villages of Judea, into other parts of the world, they drew the aforesaid genealogy from memory and from the book of daily records as faithfully as possible.
what_it_says: The 'Desposyni' (relatives of the Lord), from Nazara and Cochaba, kept private genealogical records or memorised them, and carried the genealogy to other lands.
limits: Africanus says the Desposyni were relatives 'according to the flesh' and kept records from memory; the text does not say which Mary-line (if any) was included or that Mary was among them.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.15 (Loeb section 15)
original: εἴτ' οὖν οὕτως εἴτ' ἄλλως ἔχοι, σαφεστέραν ἐξήγησιν οὐκ ἂν ἔχοι τις ἄλλος ἐξευρεῖν, ὡς ἔγωγε νομίζω πᾶς τε ὃς εὐγνώμων τυγχάνει, καὶ ἡμῖν αὕτη μελέτω, εἰ καὶ ἀμάρτυρός ἐστιν, τῷ μὴ κρείττονα ἢ ἀληθεστέραν ἔχειν εἰπεῖν· τό γέ τοι εὐαγγέλιον πάντως ἀληθεύει.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: Whether then the case stand thus or not no one could find a clearer explanation, according to my own opinion and that of every candid person. And let this suffice us, for, although we can urge no testimony in its support, we have nothing better or truer to offer. In any case the Gospel states the truth.
what_it_says: Africanus admits his solution has no testimony (ἀμάρτυρος) in support, but says it is the best available explanation.
limits: This is Africanus's own admission that the solution is unattested by any witness; he presents it as the best available explanation, not as proven.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.17 (Loeb section 17; Eusebius's own words after 'Thus far Africanus')
original: Τοσαῦτα ὁ Ἀφρικανός. καὶ δὴ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ ὧδέ πως γενεαλογουμένου, δυνάμει καὶ ἡ Μαρία σὺν αὐτῷ πέφηνεν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς οὖσα φυλῆς, εἴ γε κατὰ τὸν Μωυσέως νόμον οὐκ ἐξῆν ἑτέραις ἐπιμίγνυσθαι φυλαῖς· ἑνὶ γὰρ τῶν ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ δήμου καὶ πατριᾶς τῆς αὐτῆς ζεύγνυσθαι πρὸς γάμον παρακελεύεται, ὡς ἂν μὴ περιστρέφοιτο τοῦ γένους ὁ κλῆρος ἀπὸ φυλῆς ἐπὶ φυλήν. ὧδὶ μὲν οὖν καὶ ταῦτα ἐχέτω.
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: Thus far Africanus. And the lineage of Joseph being thus traced, Mary also is virtually shown to be of the same tribe with him, since, according to the law of Moses, intermarriages between different tribes were not permitted. For the command is to marry one of the same family and lineage, so that the inheritance may not pass from tribe to tribe. This may suffice here.
what_it_says: Eusebius himself (not Africanus) concludes that, if Joseph's lineage is traced, Mary is 'virtually' (δυνάμει) of the same tribe, because Moses's law required marriage within the tribe.
limits: The claim is TRIBE, not explicitly the house of David; Eusebius says 'virtually' (δυνάμει) and 'if indeed' (εἴ γε). Africanus says nothing about Mary here. Heli is not named as Mary's father.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides
date: Africanus c. 220-240 AD (as the brief states); Eusebius c. 311-325 AD
ref: Eusebius HE 1.7.16 (Loeb section 16, end of Africanus's letter)
original: καὶ ἐπὶ τέλει δὲ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπιστολῆς προστίθησι ταῦτα· “Ματθὰν ὁ ἀπὸ Σολομῶνος ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰακώβ. Ματθὰν ἀποθανόντος, Μελχὶ ὁ ἀπὸ Νάθαν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς γυναικὸς ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἡλί. ὁμομήτριοι ἄρα ἀδελφοὶ Ἡλὶ καὶ Ἰακώβ. Ἡλὶ ἀτέκνου ἀποθανόντος ὁ Ἰακὼβ ἀνέστησεν αὐτῷ σπέρμα, γεννήσας τὸν Ἰωσήφ, κατὰ φύσιν μὲν ἑαυτῷ, κατὰ νόμον δὲ τῷ Ἡλί. οὕτως ἀμφοτέρων ἦν υἱὸς ὁ Ἰωσήφ.”
original_edition: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, ed. K. Lake, Loeb 1926 vol. 1 (Greek text = Schwartz, GCS, as the preface states); Greek read from the PDF page image
english: And at the end of the same epistle he adds these words: Matthan, who was descended from Solomon, begot Jacob. And when Matthan was dead, Melchi, who was descended from Nathan begot Eli by the same woman. Eli and Jacob were thus uterine brothers. Eli having died childless, Jacob raised up seed to him, begetting Joseph, his own son by nature, but by law the son of Eli. Thus Joseph was the son of both.
what_it_says: Africanus's summary: Joseph is son of both Jacob (by nature) and Eli (by law); Eli and Jacob were uterine brothers.
limits: Summary of the same claim as items 3-5; no reference to Mary.

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio I (Migne PG 22, approx. cols. 880; Greek 'Α'' heading)
original: Πόθεν τὸν Χριστὸν ὡς υἱὸν Δαβὶδ γενεαλογοῦσι; πάντως ὅτι διὰ τὸν Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἐκ Δαβὶδ γεγονότα· ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ ὁ Χριστὸς, ἀλλ' ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ Μαρίας, ὡς φησιν ἡ Γραφή· ἐχρῆν τοίνυν τὴν Μαρίαν γενεαλογεῖν, εἴπερ τὸν Χριστὸν γενεαλογεῖν ἐβούλοντο, ἀλλ' οὐ τὸν Ἰωσὴφ
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: Whence do they trace Christ as son of David? Surely because of Joseph, who was descended from David; but Christ is not from Joseph but from the Holy Spirit and Mary, as Scripture says. Therefore it was necessary to trace Mary's genealogy, if they wanted to trace Christ's, and not Joseph's.
page: Migne PG 22 approx. col. 880 (Latin facing: 'Cur evangelistae Josephi, non autem Mariae, genus ascribant')
edition: Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series graeca 22 (1857)
what_it_says: The Epitome's first question: why the evangelists give Joseph's genealogy for Christ and not Mary's, since Christ is not Joseph's son.
limits: A question the text raises, not an answer; it says Mary's genealogy 'would have been needed' and does not give one. Edited Greek from the Google scan (text layer missing; OCR unusable).

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio I, opening of solution (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 881-882; Latin 'Temere igitur evangelistae')
original: τὴν Μαρίαν οὐδεὶς λόγος ἀποδείκνυσιν ἀπὸ Δαβὶδ γενομένην· μάτην ἄρα τὸν Χριστὸν ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ θρυλλοῦσι, μήτε τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ ὄντα υἱὸν, μήτε τῆς Μαρίας ἀπὸ Δαβὶδ γενεαλογουμένης· τοιαῦτα μὲν τινα τὸ πρῶτον τῶν ἠπορημένων περιεῖχε· λύσις δ' ἀνεῖη αὐτῷ ἥδε.
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: No account demonstrates that Mary was descended from David. In vain, then, do they proclaim Christ from David's seed, since he is not Joseph's son and Mary has not been traced from David. Such, at first, is what the problem contains; the solution is as follows.
what_it_says: The Epitome states as the problem that no gospel account shows Mary descended from David; the solution that follows is about the virgin birth and Joseph.
limits: The solution that follows (cols. 882-884) concerns Mary's virginity and Joseph's justice, not a genealogy of Mary. Mary's Davidic descent is therefore posed as the problem here.

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio I §8 (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 889-890; Latin §8)
original: Εἰ δὲ λέγοιτο ὑπάρχειν συγγενὴς τῆς Ἐλισάβετ, αὐτῆς μὲν οὔσης ἐκ φυλῆς Ἰούδα, τῆς τε Ἐλισάβετ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Λευί, μὴ θαυμάσῃς· πᾶν γὰρ τὸ Ἰουδαίων ἔθνος ἑνὸς ἦν γένους, αἱ τε φυλαὶ πᾶσαι ἀλλήλων συγγενεῖς· ἔνθεν καὶ ὁ θεῖος Ἀπόστολος συγγενεῖς αὐτοῦ πάντας ὀνομάζει Ἰουδαίους· ... καὶ ἄλλως δὲ εἰκὸς ἀπὸ τόπου συγγενίδα τῆς Μαρίας κεχλῆσθαι τὴν Ἐλισάβετ, διὰ τὸ οἰκεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς Ἰούδα φυλῆς ἀφ' ἧς ὡρμᾶτο ἡ Μαρία.
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: If someone says Elisabeth was a kinswoman of Mary, although Mary was of the tribe of Judah and Elisabeth of the tribe of Levi, do not be surprised: the whole nation of the Jews was one stock, and all the tribes were kin to one another. ... And besides, it is reasonable that Elisabeth was called Mary's kinswoman from the place, because she lived in the tribe of Judah, from which Mary came.
page: Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 889-890 (Latin: 'Cum tamen illa de tribu Judae, Elisabetha de Levitica fuerit; ne mireris')
what_it_says: The Epitome answers the question 'how is Elisabeth Mary's kinswoman?' by saying Elisabeth was of Levi and Mary of Judah, and the kinship is by nation and by living in Judah's tribe.
limits: Says Mary's tribe is Judah; does not say Mary was a Levite or of Aaron. Assigns Elisabeth to Levi (the Greek 'Lege δέ' footnote notes a variant).

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio I §7 (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 889; Latin §7)
original: ὅτε τοίνυν ὁ Ἰωσὴφ φυλῆς γεγονὼς ἀποδείκνυται Ἰούδα, κλήρου τε καὶ πατριᾶς Δαβὶδ, πῶς οὐχ ἕπεται καὶ τῇ Μαρίᾳ ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρᾶσθαι;
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: Since Joseph is shown to be of the tribe of Judah and of the lot and family of David, how does it not follow that Mary is also seen to be from the same?
page: Migne PG 22 approx. col. 889 (Latin §7: 'Si Josephus igitur de Judae tribu deque Davidis gente et familia fuisse demonstratur, cur non sequitur ut Maria ex iisdem originibus prodire videatur?')
what_it_says: The Epitome argues from the Mosaic rule of in-tribe, in-family marriage: if Joseph is shown to be of Judah and David's family, Mary (his wife) must be too.
limits: The argument depends on Joseph's descent and on the marriage law (Num 36); it is an inference from Joseph's line to Mary's, not a Mary genealogy.

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio I §9 and conclusion (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 891-892; Latin 'Ergo perspicue ... Mariam de genere Davidis vere derivari')
original: Δεδεῖχθαι τοίνυν σαφῶς ἡγοῦμαι, ὅτι μὴ μάτην ὁ Ἰωσὴφ ἐγενεαλογεῖτο παρὰ τοῖς θαυμασίοις τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἀποστόλοις, καὶ ὅπως ἡ Μαρία ἐκ σπέρματος οὖσα τοῦ Δαβὶδ συνίσταται, ὅ τε ἐξ αὐτῆς γεγεννημένος Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ.
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: Therefore I consider it clearly shown that Joseph's genealogy was not in vain recounted by our Saviour's admirable apostles, and how Mary, being of David's seed, is established, and Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born of her.
page: Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 891-892 (Latin: 'Mariam de genere Davidis vere derivari'; 'cum Maria desponsata ... de domo familiaque Davidis esse')
what_it_says: The Epitome states that Mary is of David's seed (ἐκ σπέρματος οὖσα τοῦ Δαβὶδ), proved by Luke's 'Joseph ... with Mary ... of the house and family of David' (Lk 2:4-5) and Gabriel's 'the throne of David his father' (Lk 1:32); Joseph's apostolic genealogy is thereby justified.
limits: The explicit Davidic claim is for MARY and rests on Joseph's house (Lk 2:4-5) plus Gabriel's words; it does not say Luke's genealogy is Mary's, and does not name Heli as her father. The Eusebian attribution is the editors' (Mai/Migne title) and was not independently checked.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio II §1 (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 892-894; Latin 'Cur alter evangelista superne ab Abrahamo exorsus deducat genealogiam')
original: Διὰ τί ὁ μὲν Ματθαῖος ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἄρξάμενος κατάγει τὴν γενεαλογίαν, ὁ δὲ Λουκᾶς τὴν ἐναντίαν τούτου βαδίσας, ἤρξατο μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ, ἀνάγει δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν Ἀδὰμ καὶ τὸν Θεόν·
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: Why does Matthew, beginning from Abraham, trace the genealogy downward, while Luke, taking the opposite course, begins from Joseph and leads upward to Adam and God?
page: Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 892-894 (page header read at low resolution; verify)
what_it_says: The Epitome's second question: Matthew runs down from Abraham, Luke runs up from Joseph to Adam and God.
limits: Luke is said to start from Joseph, not from Mary; the Epitome does not identify Luke's line as Mary's.

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Epitome, Quaestio IV §1 (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 899-900; Africanus's letter, opening portion)
original: Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἤτοι τὴν εὐαγγελικὴν ἱστορίαν ἠγνοηκότες ἢ συνεῖναι μὴ δυνηθέντες, δοξολογοῦσι πλάνῃ τὴν ἀγνοίαν ἐπύκνωσαν εἰπόντες ὅτι δικαίως γέγονεν ἡ διαφορὰ αὕτη τῶν ὀνομάτων καταριθμήσεώς τε καὶ ἐπιμιξία τῶν τε ἱερατικῶν ὡς οἷόν τε καὶ τῶν βασιλικῶν·
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image
english: Those who either do not know the evangelical history or are unable to understand it, pile up their ignorance with misleading praise, saying that this difference in the counting of names and the mixing of priestly and royal (names) happened rightly ...
page: Migne PG 22 approx. col. 900 (Latin heading: 'Africani super genealogia quae in sacris Evangeliis est')
what_it_says: The Epitome's copy of Africanus's letter opens with Africanus's criticism of those who say the mixing of priestly and royal names is deliberate; this opening is absent from HE 1.7.
limits: Mai/Migne's note (item 20) says this opening is missing from HE 1.7. No mention of Mary in the stretch read. Only the opening was read here, not the whole Epitome text.

work: Quaestiones evangelicae ad Stephanum (Epitome selecta / Ekloge), attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (attributed; the epitome is by an unnamed excerptor per the Migne/Mai title)
date: Eusebius c. 320s AD (attributed); epitome undated
ref: Editorial note (12) to the Epitome's Quaestio IV (Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 899-900)
original: De hac celebri Africani ad Aristidem epistola videndum in primis Eusebius Hist. eccl. lib. 1, 7, qui ejus partem ingentem refert, a Nicephoro postea Callisto Hist. lib. 1, 11, repetitam. Videndi insuper Hieronymus comment. ad Matth. 1, 16; Augustinus Retract. lib. 2, 7; Photius cod. 34, p. 22; denique etiam Zacharias Chrysopol. in Bib. PP. Lugd. t. XIX, p. 751, in fin.
original_edition: Migne PG 22 (Google scan, 1857), Epitome selecta ex compositis ab Eusebio ad Stephanum, after Mai (Nova PP Bibl. IV); read from PDF page image. Note is Latin (editor's), not Greek.
english: (own translation) On this famous letter of Africanus to Aristides one should look first at Eusebius, Church History 1.7, who gives a large part of it, and which Nicephorus Callistus repeated later at 1.11. One should also look at Jerome, commentary on Matthew 1:16; Augustine, Retractations 2.7; Photius, codex 34, p. 22; and finally Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis vol. 19, p. 751, at the end.
page: Migne PG 22 approx. cols. 899-900, editorial note 12
what_it_says: The editors list the pre-1500 witnesses to Africanus's letter: Eusebius HE 1.7, Nicephorus Callistus 1.11, Jerome on Matt 1:16, Augustine Retractations 2.7, Photius cod. 34, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus.
limits: Editorial list, not a witness itself. Items beyond Eusebius were NOT checked here.

work: Brief des Julius Africanus an Aristides (Spitta 1877), footnote on the restored HE 1.7 fragment
author: Friedrich Spitta (editor); reports John of Damascus's reading
date: Spitta 1877; Damascene 8th c. AD
ref: Spitta 1877, p. 77 n. 1 (PDF p. 90); reports 'Damascenus liest' for HE 1.7.17
original: καὶ δὴ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ οὕτως γενεαλογουμένου, δυνάμει καὶ ἡ παρθένος αὕτη καὶ θεοτόκος Μαρία τῆς αὐτῆς οὖσα φυλῆς
original_edition: Spitta's footnote text as read from the PDF text layer (not image-checked); Damascene quotation as Spitta gives it
english: (own translation) And so, with Joseph thus traced, virtually also this virgin and God-bearer Mary, being of the same tribe.
edition: Friedrich Spitta, Brief des Julius Africanus an Aristides, Halle: Waisenhaus 1877 (archive.org briefdesjuliusaf00spit)
what_it_says: John of Damascus, as Spitta reports, read the HE 1.7.17 sentence with 'this virgin and God-bearer' (θεοτόκος) added, which is a textual variant.
limits: Confirms that the Mary-tribe sentence was read early as referring to Mary, but Damascene still says 'tribe'. The Oratio in which Damascene reads this is not identified in the footnote as read. Spitta's text is a reconstruction; the PDF text layer is noisy.

work: Narrative of Events Happening in Persia on the Birth of Christ (ANF Africanus page)
author: Attributed to Julius Africanus (disputed; ANF intro quotes Migne's preface rejecting Africanus authorship)
date: Date disputed
ref: ANF vol. 6, 'Narrative of Events Happening in Persia on the Birth of Christ' (no section numbering)
original_edition: not read in original; English only
english: And we said to the mother: What are you named, O renowned mother? And she says: Mary, masters. And we said to her: From where are you sprung? And she replies: From this district of the Bethlehemites. Then said we: Have you not had a husband? And she answers: I was only betrothed with a view to the marriage covenant, my thoughts being far removed from this.
translator: not stated on the page read (ANF vol. 6; edited by Roberts and Donaldson)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6 (New Advent online text)
what_it_says: In this attributed narrative, Mary says she comes from the district of Bethlehem and was betrothed to a husband; no genealogy or tribe is given.
limits: Gives place (Bethlehem), not lineage or tribe; Mary is not said to be of David. Authorship is disputed in the ANF introduction, which quotes Migne's preface denying Africanus wrote it. Greek/Syriac source not checked.
